# Ribbon Scope

## How To Build

A RibbonScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The ribbon along the top of the main window: tabs, each holding the application's commands for one area of work in labelled groups.

### Shape

#### Description

A ribbon runs along the top of the window, in the colours of the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope), a row of tabs, 32 pixels tall, above the command area. The tabs are flat: each is only its label, with 8 pixels either side of it, and no borders, no rounded corners, and no line anywhere, neither between the tabs nor between the tab row and the commands. The tab row has a background of its own, a step lighter than the command area, #333333 in dark mode; a closed tab has no background, and an open tab takes the command area's background, #222222 in dark mode, so it and the commands beneath it read as one piece, the edge of the colour the only edge. In light mode the same steps run the other way, the tab row a step darker than the command area. Opening and closing tabs never shifts a label.
A tab whose commands work on one of the chat input's modes, as the Code and Spec tabs do, takes that mode's colour: its label is in the mode's colour while the tab is closed, and while open, the tab is tinted with it instead and its label is the tab's own colour. Each such tab says more. Its tabs are, in order: Project, Code, Spec, Research, and Application. The window always opens on Project. Beneath the tabs, the selected tab's commands sit in groups. There is no raw output view and no toggle for one.

#### Keyboard

<Alt+1> opens the first tab, <Alt+2> the second, and so on, through each tab in the order the tabs are shown, <Alt+5> opening Application. Each opens its tab alone, as clicking it does, and expands the ribbon first if it is collapsed. A number past the last tab does nothing. Like the ribbon's other shortcuts, they do nothing while an inset panel is open. A tab's tooltip doesn't give its shortcut, since a tab has no tooltip.

#### Opening Several Tabs

Clicking a tab opens it alone, as usual. Ctrl+clicking one (Cmd+click on macOS) opens it alongside whichever tabs are already open, or, if it is already open, closes it, so any number of tabs can be open at once. The last open tab can't be closed this way: Ctrl+clicking it leaves it open. Every open tab shows as selected.
The command area then holds the groups of every open tab side by side, in the order of the tabs rather than the order they were opened, with the same divider between one tab's groups and the next as between any groups. An open tab with no commands adds nothing, and "No commands yet" shows only when none of the open tabs has any. When the groups are wider than the window, the command area scrolls sideways. The command area stays the same height however many tabs are open.
Double-clicking a tab still collapses the ribbon, and expanding it again shows the same tabs open. Which tabs are open isn't kept between

##### Launches

the window always opens with only Project open.

#### Left Container

At the left end of the bar, left of the tab bar itself rather than inside it, so the tab bar's own padding and bottom line don't reach it, sits the left container. It holds, in order, the project indicator, the collapse chevron, and the activity spinner, and can hold other things after them. It is the same whether the ribbon is expanded, beside the tabs, or collapsed, leading the row of primary commands.
It runs from the top of the bar down to the line along its bottom, never over it, so it is the same height expanded and collapsed. Everything in it is vertically centred in that height, with no gap between one thing and the next and no padding around them: each thing's own size is all the room it takes. The container shrinks to fit what it holds, and when it holds nothing, it isn't there at all.

#### Right Container

At the right end of the bar, right of the tabs, or of the primary commands when the ribbon is collapsed, sits the right container. It holds nothing yet, and can hold other things. It lays out what it holds as the left container does: vertically centred, with no gap between things and no padding around them, shrinking to fit, and not there at all while it holds nothing, as it is now.

#### Activity

The indicator and list of the [RunningActivityScope](../../../scope/running-activity/index.md#running-activity-scope) sit in the left container, just right of the collapse chevron. While nothing is running, the spinner isn't there, and the left container shrinks around the project indicator and the chevron.

#### Project Indicator

The [ProjectIndicator](../project-indicator/index.md#project-indicator) leads the left container, a solid block the full height of the bar down to the line along its bottom, ending on that line. It is the same height, and what it shows is in the same place, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed. There is no divider between it and what

##### Follows

the change of background is the edge. The collapse chevron

sits just after it, and the activity spinner just after the chevron.

#### Groups

Groups have no titles shown. They sit side by side, and between one group and the next, 4 pixels from the buttons either side, stands a

##### Divider

a bar 4 pixels wide, in the tab row's background colour, as

tall as the buttons, from the top of the first to the bottom of the last, with its ends softly rounded. The first group starts 8 pixels from the command area's left edge. Each group still has a name, saying what its commands have in common, which is the divider's tooltip and what assistive technology reads for it.

#### Tabs

Each tab is a scope of its own, which says what groups and commands it holds, and what each command does.

##### Project

##### Code

##### Spec

- small: only in the collapsed ribbon: 22 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label, and only as wide as they are

A button's label is in the regular text colour, its icon beside or above it in the same colour, with 8 pixels either side of them. A full button always stands alone. A slim button fills only its column's width: nowhere does a button stretch to fill a row.
Every command starts from the top of its group, so the commands of a tab all start at the same line. A full button is always two slim buttons stacked tall, never shorter or taller, however much its icon and label would take, alone or beside any column.
Every button is square, with no rounded corners, and no border. A command's tooltip explains what it does rather than repeating its label, and gives its keyboard shortcut if it has one.
A command can be marked primary; each tab says which of its commands are.
A command that can't run is disabled, not hidden, and its tooltip says why.

Since no column holds more than two slim buttons, and a full button is two slim buttons tall, the tallest the command area gets is two slim buttons with 4 pixels between them, padded: 74 pixels, and never more. There are 8 pixels of padding at either end, and "No commands yet" keeps 8 pixels from the left edge too.

The chevron button is square, 22 pixels on each side, its icon centred in it. It is the same size, and its icon the same size, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed: only the way the chevron points changes.
Collapsed, the tabs go away too. Every one is only as wide as its own icon and label, 8 pixels from the next, whatever the tab it comes from calls it; a command that is slim in its tab doesn't grow to fill the row. They keep the order of their tabs, with a thin vertical divider between the commands of one tab and the next, and keep their tooltips and disabled states. The right container, when it holds anything, ends the row. Every control in the row, the dividers and the containers' contents included, is vertically centred in it.

The containers stay where they are, never scrolled away or squeezed, and nothing in the row shrinks to fit.

# Ribbon Application Tab Scope

## How To Build

A RibbonApplicationTabScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonApplicationTabScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The ribbon's Application tab: the commands for the application itself, rather than the project.

### Shape

#### Description

The Application tab of the ribbon, last of the tabs.

#### Groups

```
appearance: An "Appearance" group holds the Brightness command, its one control; there is no Dark mode switch, since the slider reaches both modes.
preferences: A "Preferences" group holds the Settings command.
```

#### Commands

```
brightness: A "Brightness" slider, which runs the whole interface from its darkest to its lightest: a moon icon, then a horizontal slider 120 pixels wide, then a sun icon, with nothing showing the setting as a number. As a ribbon setting, it has no background of its own, and sits straight on the commands' area, as tall as a slim button. Its tooltip says it makes the whole interface darker or lighter, from its darkest to its lightest, keeping its contrast, and that double-clicking it resets it.
  Its one track runs through every appearance the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope) allows, darkest first: dark mode from its darkest brightness to its lightest, then light mode from its darkest to its lightest, one position for each step, with no switch between them. So all the way left is dark mode at its darkest, and all the way right light mode at its lightest; dragging past dark mode's lightest step changes the window to light mode, and back.
  Dragging it changes the mode and the brightness straight away as it moves, and once it is let go saves the mode showing and each mode's brightness among the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope). A mode that can't be saved shows a notification titled "Could not save brightness", with why; a brightness that can't be saved fails quietly. Its thumb follows the appearance showing, however that was changed, such as from the palette, but not while it is being dragged.
  Double-clicking anywhere on it, its icons or its track, puts the mode showing back to its brightness at 0, keeping the mode, and saves it; the second click doesn't also move the thumb.
  It is primary, so the collapsed ribbon keeps it: its icons and track as they are, only as wide as they are, as tall as a small button.
settings: A "Settings" button with a gear icon. Clicking it opens the [SettingsWindowScope](../../../../scope/settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope), where the system prompt each chat tab sends is edited. Its tooltip says so, and gives its keyboard shortcut, Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS).
  It is primary, and a full button.
```

# Theme Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The look every part of the application shares: a gentle, neutral grey interface in the manner of Photoshop, Maya, or Houdini, where contrast alone says what matters, and colour is kept for meaning.

### Shape

#### Description

The theme is defined by its dark mode, built around a base grey of #444444. Dark mode is the reference: every colour below is chosen for it first, and light mode is its reasonable interpretation on a light base, keeping the same roles, the same order, and steps of about the same size. The greys are true neutrals, with no hint of blue or warmth. There are no gradients, and no texture. Everything that uses a colour names its role here rather than a value of its own, so the two modes stay coherent.

#### Hierarchy

How far a colour is from the base, in contrast, says how much it stands out, and that holds everywhere. The base is the quiet ground of the window. A step away is structure: panels, controls, and the lines between them. Further away is what is worked on: text, content, and the wells that hold it. Furthest away is state and meaning: what is selected, focused, or needs attention. Nothing structural is ever further from the base than the content it frames, and nothing decorative is ever as far as state. A hover is always a smaller step than a selection, and a selection a smaller step than focus.

#### Surfaces

Each surface in dark mode, then light mode:

- well, #2e2e2e, then #f5f5f5: where content is read or written, such as the editor, code blocks, answers, and task tables' bodies; the most contrast with the text it holds
- recessed, #383838, then #e8e8e8: text inputs, lists, and trees, a step toward the well
- base, #444444, then #d0d0d0: the window, its panels, and the sidebar; the ribbon has its own, as its scope says
- raised, #4e4e4e, then #dadada: buttons, tab bars, headers, and cards, a small step toward the viewer
- hover, #585858, then #e2e2e2: a raised or listed thing under the pointer, one step further along the way it is already raised
- pressed, #3c3c3c, then #c6c6c6: a control held down, a step back past the base
- selected, #5e5e5e, then #bcbcbc: a selected row or tab without focus, the neutral state furthest from its surface short of the accent
- overlay, #4a4a4a, then #dcdcdc: floating surfaces, such as menus, popovers, tooltips, the completion menu, and inset panels

#### Light Mode

Light mode reads the dark ladder on a light base of #d0d0d0. Wells and inputs go lighter, toward white, so they keep the most contrast with the dark text they hold, just as they are darker in dark mode for the same reason. Raised controls and floating surfaces go a smaller step lighter too, so they still come forward, and hover goes further the same way. Pressed and selected go darker, and so do lines. Text is dark on light.

#### Text

Text in dark mode, then light mode:

- primary, #ebebeb, then #1e1e1e: the foreground, for anything read
- secondary, #c4c4c4, then #454545: what the spec calls muted, such as paths, counts, and descriptions
- tertiary, #9c9c9c, then #636363: dimmer than muted, such as help text and placeholders
- disabled, #7a7a7a, then #8c8c8c: what can't be used now

#### Lines

Lines are one pixel, and quieter than anything they separate:

- line, #3a3a3a, then #bdbdbd: dividers between areas, table rows, and list rows
- edge, #2a2a2a, then #a6a6a6: the border of controls, inputs, and floating surfaces, darker than the base in both modes, what the spec calls the border colour

A line is never doubled. Wherever two things that each have a border meet, a single line is drawn between them, never two side by side: one of them leaves that side out, or the two overlap so their lines lie on the same pixels. A thing that fills what holds it leaves out the sides the holder already draws, and a row in a stack draws only the line between it and the row before. This holds while things move too, such as a row sliding into a stack, apart from a frame or two. A focus ring, or an accent bar marking what is current, isn't a border in this sense, and may sit against one. A gpui-kit component used with its default styling, such as tabs in a tab bar, keeps its own borders as gpui-kit draws them; only its colours are the theme's.

#### Accent

One accent, a calm blue, is the only colour that means selection, focus, or the primary action:

- accent, #7fb4ea, then #1f5fa6: focus rings, the underline of a selected tab, links, a selection's edge, and accent text
- accent fill, #3d6a98, then #2b68ad: primary buttons, with primary text in white in both modes, and a selected item in a focused list
- selection, the accent fill at 35% over its surface: selected text

What the spec calls the theme's primary colour, or its focus ring colour, is the accent.

#### Status

Status colours are kept for what they mean, readable as text on the base and every surface darker than it in dark mode, and on the base and every surface lighter than it in light mode:

- success, #8fd095, then #2c6e31: done, added, aligned
- warning, #e6bb68, then #8a5a00: running out, modified, drifting
- error, #f0928a, then #b3261e: failed, removed, diverged
- information, the accent: running, informational notes

Two more hues, for telling kinds of things apart rather than for status:

- purple, #bba0e6, then #6b4aa6
- cyan, #78c8ce, then #1f6f78

Wherever the spec names a hue for what is shown, it means the theme's: blue is the accent, green success, amber or yellow warning, red error, purple and cyan the hues above, and grey tertiary text.
A tint of a colour, such as a prompt mode's or a changed line's, is that colour laid over its surface at low strength, never enough to take the text on it below its contrast.

#### Bevel

A surface that should lift slightly off what it sits on, such as a table's header or a hovered scrollbar button, can have the theme's bevel: a very slight 1 pixel edge around it, just enough to lift it. Its top and left edges are a touch lighter, as white laid faintly over the surface, 8% in dark mode and 55% in light mode; its bottom and right edges only barely darker, as black laid very faintly over it, 6% in dark mode and 3% in light mode, far subtler than the light and never reading as a line. Laid over rather than a colour of its own, it looks the same on any surface, hovered, pressed, or tinted. The lit top runs the full width, and the lit left side runs beneath it; the shaded bottom runs the full width, and the shaded right side runs above it, so no two edges overlap. It sits inside the surface, taking no room, and isn't a border in the sense of lines never being doubled.
A surface being pressed in can have the bevel pressed instead: the same edges, with the light and shade swapped, so its top and left edges are barely darker and its bottom and right edges a touch lighter.

#### Elevation

Floating surfaces sit on the overlay surface with an edge border, and are the only things with a shadow: soft, short, and black, stronger in dark mode than in light. Behind a modal surface, such as an inset panel, the window is dimmed with black, 40% in dark mode and 25% in light mode.

#### Contrast

However the colours are used, primary and secondary text keep at least 4.5 to 1 against the base, recessed, well, and overlay surfaces, and primary text at least 4 to 1 on controls in any state. Tertiary text, status colours, and the accent keep at least 3 to 1 on the base. Edges keep about 1.5 to 1 against the base, and lines less.

#### Brightness

The whole interface can be made lighter or darker, from the Brightness slider of the ribbon's Application tab, without changing how it reads. Brightness moves the mode's whole ladder of neutral greys together, by the same amount in lightness, every surface, line, bevel, and overlay with it: the ribbon's greys, the file tree's darkest surface, the wells, the base, raised, hover, pressed, and selected surfaces, and the scrollbar's track, since it is laid over them. The steps between them stay the size they are at 0, and their order never changes: in dark mode what is lighter than what it sits on stays lighter, however bright it is made, and in light mode what is darker stays darker. A raised box never becomes darker than its ground, nor a well lighter than the base.
Each mode has its own brightness, running from -10 to +10, each step moving every channel of every grey by 2% of the way from black to white, rounded to a whole value, but only as far as the mode allows: a mode's brightness stops at whichever step would first push a grey below black or above white, since clipping would close the steps up, or bring text or a hue below the contrast asked of it above. At 0 the greys are exactly those given above. With these greys, dark mode runs from -3 to +1 and light mode from -4 to +2.
The Brightness slider runs through both modes as one scale, dark mode's steps from its darkest to its lightest, then light mode's, so the interface goes from its darkest to its lightest with no switch between modes. Where it crosses from dark mode's lightest step to light mode's darkest, the greys jump, the base from about #494949 to #bcbcbc, rather than blending through the mid greys between, on which neither mode's text would keep its contrast.
Text keeps its colours as the greys move, unless moving them would bring it below that contrast, in which case the brightness stops there rather than recolouring it. The accent, the mode colours, and the status colours keep their hues; tints laid over a surface, such as a mode's, are laid over the moved surface and so move with it. Everything takes the new brightness at once, while the slider is dragged, with no flicker and nothing laid out anew.

#### Gpui Kit

The application's gpui-kit theme is set from these roles in both modes, so a component with gpui-kit's default styling follows the theme with nothing of its own: its background is the base, its foreground primary text, its muted foreground secondary text, its border the edge, its input and list backgrounds recessed, its popover the overlay, its primary and ring the accent, and its success, warning, and danger the status colours.

#### Modes

Which mode shows is up to the application: see the [MainWindowScope](../../scope/application/MainWindow.md#main-window-scope).

Wherever two things that each have a border meet, a single line is drawn between them, never two side by side: one of them leaves that side out, or the two overlap so their lines lie on the same pixels. A thing that fills what holds it leaves out the sides the holder already draws, and a row in a stack draws only the line between it and the row before. This holds while things move too, such as a row sliding into a stack, apart from a frame or two. A focus ring, or an accent bar marking what is current, isn't a border in this sense, and may sit against one. A gpui-kit component used with its default styling, such as tabs in a tab bar, keeps its own borders as gpui-kit draws them; only its colours are the theme's.

#### Accent

One accent, a calm blue, is the only colour that means selection, focus, or the primary action:

- accent, #7fb4ea, then #1f5fa6: focus rings, the underline of a selected tab, links, a selection's edge, and accent text
- accent fill, #3d6a98, then #2b68ad: primary buttons, with primary text in white in both modes, and a selected item in a focused list
- selection, the accent fill at 35% over its surface: selected text

What the spec calls the theme's primary colour, or its focus ring colour, is the accent.

#### Status

Status colours are kept for what they mean, readable as text on the base and every surface darker than it in dark mode, and on the base and every surface lighter than it in light mode:

- success, #8fd095, then #2c6e31: done, added, aligned
- warning, #e6bb68, then #8a5a00: running out, modified, drifting
- error, #f0928a, then #b3261e: failed, removed, diverged
- information, the accent: running, informational notes

Two more hues, for telling kinds of things apart rather than for status:

- purple, #bba0e6, then #6b4aa6
- cyan, #78c8ce, then #1f6f78

Wherever the spec names a hue for what is shown, it means the theme's: blue is the accent, green success, amber or yellow warning, red error, purple and cyan the hues above, and grey tertiary text.
A tint of a colour, such as a prompt mode's or a changed line's, is that colour laid over its surface at low strength, never enough to take the text on it below its contrast.

#### Bevel

A surface that should lift slightly off what it sits on, such as a table's header or a hovered scrollbar button, can have the theme's bevel: a very slight 1 pixel edge around it, just enough to lift it. Its top and left edges are a touch lighter, as white laid faintly over the surface, 8% in dark mode and 55% in light mode; its bottom and right edges only barely darker, as black laid very faintly over it, 6% in dark mode and 3% in light mode, far subtler than the light and never reading as a line. Laid over rather than a colour of its own, it looks the same on any surface, hovered, pressed, or tinted. The lit top runs the full width, and the lit left side runs beneath it; the shaded bottom runs the full width, and the shaded right side runs above it, so no two edges overlap. It sits inside the surface, taking no room, and isn't a border in the sense of lines never being doubled.
A surface being pressed in can have the bevel pressed instead: the same edges, with the light and shade swapped, so its top and left edges are barely darker and its bottom and right edges a touch lighter.

#### Elevation

Floating surfaces sit on the overlay surface with an edge border, and are the only things with a shadow: soft, short, and black, stronger in dark mode than in light. Behind a modal surface, such as an inset panel, the window is dimmed with black, 40% in dark mode and 25% in light mode.

#### Contrast

However the colours are used, primary and secondary text keep at least 4.5 to 1 against the base, recessed, well, and overlay surfaces, and primary text at least 4 to 1 on controls in any state. Tertiary text, status colours, and the accent keep at least 3 to 1 on the base. Edges keep about 1.5 to 1 against the base, and lines less.

#### Brightness

The whole interface can be made lighter or darker, from the Brightness slider of the ribbon's Application tab, without changing how it reads. Brightness moves the mode's whole ladder of neutral greys together, by the same amount in lightness, every surface, line, bevel, and overlay with it: the ribbon's greys, the file tree's darkest surface, the wells, the base, raised, hover, pressed, and selected surfaces, and the scrollbar's track, since it is laid over them. The steps between them stay the size they are at 0, and their order never changes: in dark mode what is lighter than what it sits on stays lighter, however bright it is made, and in light mode what is darker stays darker. A raised box never becomes darker than its ground, nor a well lighter than the base.
Each mode has its own brightness, running from -10 to +10, each step moving every channel of every grey by 2% of the way from black to white, rounded to a whole value, but only as far as the mode allows: a mode's brightness stops at whichever step would first push a grey below black or above white, since clipping would close the steps up, or bring text or a hue below the contrast asked of it above. At 0 the greys are exactly those given above. With these greys, dark mode runs from -3 to +1 and light mode from -4 to +2.
The Brightness slider runs through both modes as one scale, dark mode's steps from its darkest to its lightest, then light mode's, so the interface goes from its darkest to its lightest with no switch between modes. Where it crosses from dark mode's lightest step to light mode's darkest, the greys jump, the base from about #494949 to #bcbcbc, rather than blending through the mid greys between, on which neither mode's text would keep its contrast.
Text keeps its colours as the greys move, unless moving them would bring it below that contrast, in which case the brightness stops there rather than recolouring it. The accent, the mode colours, and the status colours keep their hues; tints laid over a surface, such as a mode's, are laid over the moved surface and so move with it. Everything takes the new brightness at once, while the slider is dragged, with no flicker and nothing laid out anew.

#### Gpui Kit

The application's gpui-kit theme is set from these roles in both modes, so a component with gpui-kit's default styling follows the theme with nothing of its own: its background is the base, its foreground primary text, its muted foreground secondary text, its border the edge, its input and list backgrounds recessed, its popover the overlay, its primary and ring the accent, and its success, warning, and danger the status colours.

#### Modes

Which mode shows is up to the application: see the [MainWindowScope](../../scope/application/MainWindow.md#main-window-scope).

# Inset Panel Scope

## How To Build

A InsetPanelScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A InsetPanelScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

A floating panel over the whole main window, for work that needs more room than a popup and shouldn't disturb what is beneath it.

### Shape

#### Description

The panel floats over everything in the window, the ribbon and sidebar included, inset 32 pixels from every edge of the window. It has rounded corners, a border, and a shadow, and whatever it holds fills it. The window behind it is dimmed, and nothing behind it takes the mouse while it is open. Only one panel is open at a time.

#### Animating

The panel comes in each time it opens and goes away each time it closes with the [RiseInAnimation](../../animations/rise-in/index.md#rise-in-animation): the panel is its surface, and the dimmed window around the panel is its dimming. Switching what the panel holds, such as opening a diff while the settings are open, swaps it in place.

#### Modal

While the panel is open, nothing beneath it can take focus or input; only the panel and what it holds can.
The mouse can't reach anything beneath: no clicks, scrolling, hovering, or tooltips, except that clicking the dimmed window closes the panel.
Focus moves into the panel when it opens and can't leave it. <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> cycle through what can be focused within the panel, going round from the last back to the first and the other way, rather than on to anything beneath. Anything that would move focus beneath while it is open, such as a task beneath finishing, sends focus back into the panel instead.
The main window's shortcuts that act on what is beneath do nothing while it is open: opening the palette with <Ctrl+P> (<Cmd+P> on macOS), and collapsing or expanding the ribbon with <Ctrl+F1> (<Cmd+F1> on macOS). Shortcuts that open something of their own, like the settings window, or quitting, still work.

#### Closing

The panel closes with a close or cancel button in what it holds, with <Escape>, or by clicking the dimmed window around it; clicking inside the panel never closes it. Once it closes, focus goes back to the chat input.
----
# User Preferences Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The choices the application remembers for the user, rather than for a project, so each launch starts as the last one left off.

### Shape

#### Description

Preferences are remembered for the user across launches and across all projects, in the platform's per-user config directory, never in a project.

#### Preferences

- light or dark mode, which, until chosen, follows the operating system's appearance
- the interface's brightness, one for dark mode and one for light, each starting at 0
- whether the ribbon is collapsed, which starts expanded
- the layout of a file's diff, which starts side by side
- the recent projects
- the folder a project was last opened from
- the harness runs go to, which starts as Claude Code

A preference is saved as soon as it is chosen, and restored on the next launch.

#### Failing

A preference that can't be saved still holds for the rest of the session. Only light or dark mode says so, as the commands that change it do; the others, brightness among them, fail quietly, being only a convenience.
-----

# Prompt Modes Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The modes a prompt is sent in, each for a different kind of work on the code and the spec.

### Shape

#### Description

There are five modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this order.

#### Modes

- Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red
- Chain: changes the code and the spec together; purple
- Spec: changes the spec, leaving the code as it is; a subtle blue
- Ask: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither; a subtle green
- Freeform: passes the prompt to the agent just as it is written; grey, the theme's tertiary text colour

#### Colours

Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's colour, a tint of the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s hue of that name, readable in both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple.

#### Tasks

A prompt sent in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform is a task, sent as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Tasks carry on one conversation, one at a time, and queue while the harness is working. Before one is sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says. Once one finishes without error, having changed files, it adds a commit note to the [GitPanelScope](../../../ui/components/git-panel/index.md#git-panel-scope).

#### Questions

A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or adds a commit note. Questions carry on a conversation of their own, apart from the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.

#### Freeform

A prompt sent in Freeform is passed to the harness exactly as it was typed, with anything attached to it, and nothing else: no system prompt, no hidden anchor compiled from it, no spec built ahead of it, no slices, whatever the Slice toggle says, and no understanding file. Otherwise it is a task like any other: it queues while the harness is working, carries on the tasks' conversation, heads the message list, is saved in the prompt history, can be cancelled or resent, and adds a commit note once it finishes having changed files. It is saved in the history as a hidden anchor like any task's, recording its mode, so the queue and history hold it as they hold the others, but that anchor is never compiled, imports nothing, and has no system prompt. Its header shows the prompt as it was sent, with no hidden anchor named, and the referenced spec sidebar doesn't slide out while it runs, since it references nothing. What is sent to a running Freeform task, from Send to task, goes just as it was typed too. It is never sent to another mode, alone or in a batch.

#### System Prompts

Each mode but Freeform sends its own system prompt, from the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope). A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while it waits in the queue.

A SettingsWindowScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details. ## Concept

### Pitch

The modes a prompt is sent in, each for a different kind of work on the code and the spec.

### Shape

#### Description

There are five modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this order.

#### Modes

- Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red
- Chain: changes the code and the spec together; purple
- Spec: changes the spec, leaving the code as it is; a subtle blue
- Ask: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither; a subtle green
- Freeform: passes the prompt to the agent just as it is written; grey, the theme's tertiary text colour

#### Colours

Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's colour, a tint of the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s hue of that name, readable in both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple.

#### Tasks

A prompt sent in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform is a task, sent as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Tasks carry on one conversation, one at a time, and queue while the harness is working. Before one is sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says. Once one finishes without error, having changed files, it adds a commit note to the [GitPanelScope](../../../ui/components/git-panel/index.md#git-panel-scope).

#### Questions

A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or adds a commit note. Questions carry on a conversation of their own, apart from the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.

#### Freeform

A prompt sent in Freeform is passed to the harness exactly as it was typed, with anything attached to it, and nothing else: no system prompt, no hidden anchor compiled from it, no spec built ahead of it, no slices, whatever the Slice toggle says, and no understanding file. Otherwise it is a task like any other: it queues while the harness is working, carries on the tasks' conversation, heads the message list, is saved in the prompt history, can be cancelled or resent, and adds a commit note once it finishes having changed files. It is saved in the history as a hidden anchor like any task's, recording its mode, so the queue and history hold it as they hold the others, but that anchor is never compiled, imports nothing, and has no system prompt. Its header shows the prompt as it was sent, with no hidden anchor named, and the referenced spec sidebar doesn't slide out while it runs, since it references nothing. What is sent to a running Freeform task, from Send to task, goes just as it was typed too. It is never sent to another mode, alone or in a batch.

#### System Prompts

Each mode but Freeform sends its own system prompt, from the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope). A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while it waits in the queue.

It opens with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS) from anywhere in the application, or from whatever command opens the settings, in place of anything else in the inset panel. Opening it while it is already open leaves it as it is rather than opening another.

#### System Prompts

The "System prompts" section is headed "System prompts", with a muted line beneath saying that each tab gives a prompt sent from it this system prompt, that they are saved with the project as they are edited, and that the CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION placeholders stand for the code and spec locations, SPEC_READING for the injected spec-reading prompt, and PITON_FLUENCY for the project's Piton fluency, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.
Then, for each tab but Freeform, which sends no system prompt, in the order of the [PromptModesScope](../prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope): its name, the muted path of the file its prompt is saved in, and a "Reset to default" button, disabled while the prompt is already the default, which puts the default back and saves it. Beneath them, an editor for the prompt, highlighting it as Piton, with soft wrapping and no line numbers or folding. The editor grows to fit the prompt, as a [GrowingTextInputScope](../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input-scope) does, with no most, so it never scrolls on its

##### Own

the whole prompt is always in it, and the page scrolls instead,

the mouse wheel over an editor scrolling the page. A prompt that can't be read or saved says why beneath its editor.
Without a project open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) says, in place of the prompts it reads "Open a project to edit its system prompts."

#### Injected Prompts

The "Injected prompts" section is headed "Injected prompts", with a muted line beneath saying that these are injected into the system prompts wherever their placeholder is written, that they are saved with the project as they are edited, and that HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for the directory of the harness in use, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.
Then the spec-reading prompt, laid out as each tab's system prompt is: its name, "Spec reading", the muted path of the file it is saved in, a "Reset to default" button, disabled while it is already the default, its editor, and why it can't be read or saved, if it can't. Beneath it the code-to-spec prompt, laid out the same way, named "Code to spec", with a muted line saying it is added to a Code task sent to Spec, and that CODE_PROMPT and CODE_RESULT stand for the code task's prompt and its final output.
Without a project open, in place of it the section reads "Open a project to edit its injected prompts."

#### Agent

The "Agent" section is headed "Agent", with a muted line beneath saying that every run, the tasks, the questions, and the application's own, goes to the harness picked here, and that a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with.
Then a row for each harness, in order: Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, each a radio button reading its name, with the command it runs muted beside it, `claude`, `codex`, or `opencode`, and "Not installed" muted after that when the command can't be found. Exactly one is picked, the harness in use, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says. Clicking one picks it; it is used from the next run on, and remembered for the user straight away, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) says, not saved with a project, so the section is the same with or without a project open. One that isn't installed can still be picked, and its runs fail saying why.

#### Saving

The prompts, the system prompts and the injected ones, belong to the project opened through the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), each saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. Every edit is saved straight away. When the window loads the prompts, any prompt with no file yet has its default saved, so every prompt can also be found and edited by hand. The prompts are read again each time the settings open and whenever another project is opened, so an edit made by hand shows up; a prompt that already shows what was read is left alone, so its cursor stays put.

#### Templates

A prompt is a template, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, and a reset puts back its default.

content.text:
The Application tab now has a **Theme** button that opens a theme editor in the inset panel. It lets you set the Base, Code, Chain, Spec and Ask colours. The suite passes except one test, `system_prompts::defaults_are_this_repositorys_templates`, which fails the same way without my changes. I haven't launched the app to look at the editor. The only UI check is a new test that opens it, sets a colour, resets it and closes it.

**How it works**
- **The button:** it sits in its own "Colours" group between Appearance and Preferences, as a full-size button with a palette icon. It isn't marked primary, so the collapsed ribbon doesn't show it.
- **The editor:** it has the same heading and close button as Settings. Each of the five colours gets a row with gpui-kit's colour picker, its hex value, a short description, and a Reset button that's disabled until you've changed that colour. At the bottom, "Reset all" puts every colour back.
- **Dark and light kept apart:** each mode keeps its own colours, since the theme's defaults differ per mode. The editor edits whichever mode is showing, and a Dark mode / Light mode toggle at the top switches between them.
- **Base colour:** this is the base at brightness 0. Every other grey keeps its distance from it, so the Brightness slider still works from there. Changing the base changes how far brightness can go, and the slider rebuilds its track to match.
- **Mode colours:** these replace the theme's red, blue and green wherever a mode is shown (chat input tabs, send button, ribbon tabs, file tree, task rows). Chain is still halfway between Code and Spec unless you set it, and the tab colour transition now passes through Chain's colour.
- **Saving:** changes show immediately and are saved to a new `colors` file next to the `theme` and `brightness` files. They're restored at launch before brightness is. As the preferences spec says for everything except dark/light mode, a failed save is ignored and the change still lasts for the session.

The changes are in `theme.rs`, `theme_preference.rs`, `chat_input.rs`, `ribbon/application_tab.rs`, `ribbon/mod.rs` and `main_window.rs`, plus the new `src/theme_editor.rs`. I added tests for moving the base, saving and loading colours, and the editor itself, and updated the ribbon test for the new group.

**Decisions for you**
- **Spec not updated:** you asked me not to edit `./spec`, so nothing there mentions the editor, the Colours group, or user-chosen colours. The theme spec currently says the greys are "true neutrals", and the picker allows a tinted base. If you want the spec to match, it needs an update.
- **Chosen colours aren't adjusted:** the theme's own colours are nudged to stay readable near the middle brightness, but colours you pick are used exactly as picked.
- **Small memory growth:** each new base colour you try keeps a small palette in memory (about 130 bytes per brightness step you view) until the app closes. This let me leave how the rest of the app reads the palette unchanged.

I ran `cargo fmt`, which also reformatted unrelated files. I reverted that, so the diff only contains this feature.
